---
title: "Polymorphism, and one class per file"
---

Every class you have written so far sits in `src/index.ts`, next to the code
that talks to the page. This chapter splits that file up, one class per file.
Before that it deals with the reason classes are worth the trouble: a program
that grows a new kind of thing should not need a new branch in ten places.

## A switch for every question {#sec-polymorphism-switch}

Create a new app `shape-switch` from our template inside `coursework/`.
Replace `src/index.ts` with this and run `npm start`:

```ts
type Shape = {
  kind: 'rect' | 'triangle';
  width: number;
  height: number;
};

const area = (shape: Shape): number => {
  switch (shape.kind) {
    case 'rect':
      return shape.width * shape.height;
    case 'triangle':
      return (shape.width * shape.height) / 2;
  }
};

const describe = (shape: Shape): string => {
  switch (shape.kind) {
    case 'rect':
      return `Rectangle ${shape.width} by ${shape.height}`;
    case 'triangle':
      return `Triangle ${shape.width} by ${shape.height}`;
  }
};

const shapes: Shape[] = [
  { kind: 'rect', width: 30, height: 20 },
  { kind: 'triangle', width: 30, height: 20 },
];

for (const shape of shapes) {
  console.log(`${describe(shape)} has area ${area(shape)}`);
}
```

Open the browser console with F12:

```
Rectangle 30 by 20 has area 600
Triangle 30 by 20 has area 300
```

Now a third kind arrives. Add `'line'` to the union in the type and one more
object to the array:

```ts
  kind: 'rect' | 'triangle' | 'line';
```

```ts
  { kind: 'line', width: 30, height: 0 },
```

Run `npm run build` and read what comes back:

```
src/index.ts(7,30): error TS2366: Function lacks ending return statement and return type does not include 'undefined'.
src/index.ts(16,34): error TS2366: Function lacks ending return statement and return type does not include 'undefined'.
```

TypeScript checked both `switch` statements and stopped the build, because
neither of them answers for a `'line'`. That part is good news. The work is
still yours though, one edit per `switch`, so two edits here. A real drawing
program also has a `draw` and a `color` function, and there one new kind costs
four edits in four places, each of them easy to forget.

## The object answers for itself {#sec-polymorphism-classes}

Delete everything in `src/index.ts` and write the same two shapes as classes:

```ts
abstract class Shape {
  abstract area(): number;
  abstract describe(): string;
}

class Rect extends Shape {
  constructor(
    private width: number,
    private height: number,
  ) {
    super();
  }

  area(): number {
    return this.width * this.height;
  }

  describe(): string {
    return `Rectangle ${this.width} by ${this.height}`;
  }
}

class Triangle extends Shape {
  constructor(
    private width: number,
    private height: number,
  ) {
    super();
  }

  area(): number {
    return (this.width * this.height) / 2;
  }

  describe(): string {
    return `Triangle ${this.width} by ${this.height}`;
  }
}

const shapes: Shape[] = [new Rect(30, 20), new Triangle(30, 20)];

for (const shape of shapes) {
  console.log(`${shape.describe()} has area ${shape.area()}`);
}
```

The console prints the same two lines as before. Now add the line, the same
third kind that just cost you two compiler errors:

```ts
class Line extends Shape {
  constructor(private length: number) {
    super();
  }

  area(): number {
    return 0;
  }

  describe(): string {
    return `Line of length ${this.length}`;
  }
}
```

Put one more object into the array and reload:

```ts
const shapes: Shape[] = [new Rect(30, 20), new Triangle(30, 20), new Line(30)];
```

```
Rectangle 30 by 20 has area 600
Triangle 30 by 20 has area 300
Line of length 30 has area 0
```

Nothing else needed a change. The loop at the bottom never learned that a
third kind exists, because `Line` brought its own `area` and its own
`describe` with it.

## The name is polymorphism {#sec-polymorphism-name}

`shape.area()` is one call in your source code, and it runs three different
method bodies depending on which object `shape` holds at that moment. "Poly"
is Greek for many and "morph" for form, so the word says many forms. One name,
many method bodies, and the object decides which body runs. This is
**polymorphism**, and the array of `Ball` objects in the previous chapter was
already doing it.

A `switch` over a `kind` field is what polymorphism replaces. Those branches
ask an object what it is so the caller can decide what to do. Give the object
a method instead and let it answer for itself. When you catch yourself writing
`switch (thing.kind)` or `if (thing.kind === 'circle')`, that is the signal.

Not every `switch` is a mistake. A `switch` over two kinds in one single place
is fine, so leave it alone. A class hierarchy earns its keep once the same set
of kinds gets asked several different questions, which is exactly what the two
calculators below do.

## One class per file {#sec-polymorphism-modules}

From here on, every class in this course gets a file of its own, named after
the class in lowercase. `Shape` lives in `src/shape.ts`, `Rect` in
`src/rect.ts`, and a two-word class such as `ToolSelection` gets a hyphen,
`src/tool-selection.ts`. Splitting the file you just wrote takes one new word.

Create `src/shape.ts` and move the abstract class into it:

```ts
export abstract class Shape {
  abstract area(): number;
  abstract describe(): string;
}
```

`export` marks a name that other files may use. Anything in a file without
`export` in front of it stays inside that file, invisible from outside. A file
with at least one `import` or `export` is called a **module**.

Now `src/rect.ts`:

```ts
import { Shape } from './shape';

export class Rect extends Shape {
  constructor(
    private width: number,
    private height: number,
  ) {
    super();
  }

  area(): number {
    return this.width * this.height;
  }

  describe(): string {
    return `Rectangle ${this.width} by ${this.height}`;
  }
}
```

The name in the braces has to match the exported name. The text after `from`
is the path to the file, and the research box below asks you to pin down what
its leading `./` means. Course style leaves the `.ts` off the end, and this
starter would accept `'./shape.ts'` too, because its `tsconfig.json` switches
`allowImportingTsExtensions` on.

Move `Triangle` and `Line` the same way, and `src/index.ts` shrinks to this:

```ts
import { Line } from './line';
import { Rect } from './rect';
import type { Shape } from './shape';
import { Triangle } from './triangle';

const shapes: Shape[] = [new Rect(30, 20), new Triangle(30, 20), new Line(30)];

for (const shape of shapes) {
  console.log(`${shape.describe()} has area ${shape.area()}`);
}
```

No class is left in `src/index.ts`. It picks the classes it needs and wires
them together, and that is the job it keeps for the rest of the year.

## Two kinds of import {#sec-polymorphism-import-type}

One of the four import lines in `src/index.ts` carries an extra word:

```ts
import type { Shape } from './shape';
```

There, the name `Shape` is only ever used as a type, in
`const shapes: Shape[]`, and types are gone by the time the browser sees your
code. Write that line as a plain `import` and Biome points at it:

```
src/index.ts:3:8 lint/style/useImportType  FIXABLE
  ! All these imports are only used as types.
```

`import type` says that you need the name for the compiler and for nothing
else, so the whole line disappears from the built code. In `src/rect.ts` the
plain `import` has to stay, because `extends Shape` reaches for the real class
while the program runs. Put a `type` in front of it there and TypeScript stops
you:

```
src/rect.ts(3,27): error TS1361: 'Shape' cannot be used as a value because it was imported using 'import type'.
```

Two rules cover every case you will meet this year. A name you use with `new`,
with `extends`, or as a value needs a plain `import`. A name that appears only
after a colon or in angle brackets takes `import type`.

## What Vite does with five files {#sec-polymorphism-vite}

Run `npm start`, open the developer tools with F12, pick the Network tab, and
reload the page. The browser asks for each file on its own: `index.ts`,
`line.ts`, `rect.ts`, `shape.ts`, and `triangle.ts`. That is the dev server
handing you one module at a time, so a change to `line.ts` reloads `line.ts`.
The finished build is a different story:

```bash
npm run build
```

```
✓ 8 modules transformed.
dist/index.html                0.33 kB │ gzip: 0.24 kB
dist/assets/index-QKlOSpwk.js  1.28 kB │ gzip: 0.58 kB
```

Five source files, one JavaScript file in `dist`. Splitting your code into
small files costs your visitors nothing.

::: {.research title="Two decimals, and where an import looks"}
Both calculators below print areas and euro amounts with exactly two decimals,
and each of them is a folder of files importing each other. Neither detail is
spelled out in this chapter.

1. An area comes out as `3216.990877275948` and you want the text `3216.99`.
   Which method of a number gives you that, and what type does the method
   return?
2. Search for `export default`. How does importing a default export differ
   from importing a named export such as `export class Rectangle`?
3. `import { Rectangle } from './rectangle';` and
   `import { defineConfig } from 'vite';` are both imports. What does the
   leading `./` say about where the file is looked for, and where does the
   search go when the `./` is missing?

Question 1 has to stick for the exam. Rounding a number for display shows up
in almost every task, and you will write it without a search engine.
:::

## Exercise A: a shapes calculator {#sec-polymorphism-exercise-shapes}

{{< exercise shapes-calculator >}}

The page is ready: five buttons with the ids `addRectangleButton`,
`addSquareButton`, `addEllipseButton`, `addCircleButton`, and `addLineButton`,
an empty `<ul id="shapesList">`, and a `<span id="totalArea">` inside the
total line. Each button adds one shape with random sizes, the list shows every
shape with its area, and the total line adds them up.

Six classes, six files. Build them in this order:

1. **`src/shape.ts`.** An abstract class `Shape` with an abstract getter
   `description` that returns a string, and a normal method `area()` that
   returns `0`. Every shape without an area of its own keeps that answer.

2. **`src/rectangle.ts`.** `Rectangle extends Shape`, with `width` and
   `height` as private parameter properties. `description` returns text like
   `Rectangle 30 by 20`, and `area()` returns width times height.

3. **`src/square.ts`.** `Square extends Rectangle`. Its constructor takes one
   side as a private parameter property of its own and hands it to `super`
   twice; `Rectangle` keeps its width and height private, so `Square` cannot
   read them. Override `description` only, so the list says
   `Square with side 7` instead of `Rectangle 7 by 7`. The area comes from
   `Rectangle` unchanged.

4. **`src/ellipse.ts`.** `Ellipse extends Shape` with `radiusX` and `radiusY`.
   `description` returns text like `Ellipse with radii 40 and 25`, and its
   area is `Math.PI * radiusX * radiusY`.

5. **`src/circle.ts`.** `Circle extends Ellipse`, one radius handed to `super`
   twice, `description` overridden.

6. **`src/line.ts`.** `Line extends Shape` with a length, and `description`
   returns text like `Line of length 60`. Write no `area()` here at all. The
   one in `Shape` already returns `0`, and that is the right answer for a line.

7. **`src/index.ts`.** Import `./styles.css` first, then the five classes you
   create objects from, and `Shape` with `import type`. Fetch the seven
   elements with `document.querySelector<...>` and throw in one `if` when
   something is missing. Keep the shapes in `const shapes: Shape[] = [];`.

8. **A render function.** Write `render` as a helper that empties
   `#shapesList` with `replaceChildren()`, then loops over `shapes` and
   appends one `<li>` per shape. A line reads
   `Circle with radius 10: area 314.16`, so the area is rounded to two
   decimals. Add the areas up on the way through and write the total into
   `#totalArea`, with two decimals as well.

9. **Five listeners.** Each `click` builds its shape with whole random numbers
   from 1 to 100, pushes it, and calls `render`. `Math.floor(Math.random() *
   100) + 1` gives you one such number.

10. **Run `npm start` and test.** Click Line five times: five entries appear,
    every one of them with `area 0.00`, and the total stays `0.00`. Then click
    Square once and check that the total is the side times itself.

11. **Run `npm run verify`** and fix what it reports.

## Exercise B: what the trip is worth {#sec-polymorphism-exercise-travel}

{{< exercise travel-costs >}}

Your company pays employees per kilometer, and how much depends on how they
travelled. The page has a distance field with the id `distanceInput`, six
buttons, a `<ul id="travelList">`, and a `<span id="totalReimbursement">`.
The rules:

| Means of transport | Reimbursement in euro |
| --- | --- |
| Car | `distance * 0.5 + passengers * 0.15` |
| Motorcycle | `distance * 0.25` |
| Bicycle | `0` up to and including 1 km, otherwise the same as a motorcycle |
| Walk | `0` up to and including 1 km, otherwise `distance * 0.38` |

`passengers` counts the people riding along, not the driver. Three buttons
create a car: `carButton` with nobody along, `carOneButton` with one, and
`carTwoButton` with two. The other three are `motorcycleButton`,
`bicycleButton`, and `walkButton`.

1. **`src/travel.ts`.** An abstract class `Travel` whose constructor takes
   `protected readonly distance: number` as a parameter property. Give it an
   abstract getter `description`, an abstract method `reimbursement(): number`,
   and one normal method `summary()` that glues both together into a line such
   as `Car, 10.00 km: 5.00 €`. Both numbers get two decimals.

2. **`src/car.ts`.** `Car extends Travel` with a second constructor parameter
   `private readonly passengers: number`. Its `description` reads `Car` for
   nobody along, `Car with 1 additional passenger` for one, and
   `Car with 2 additional passengers` for more.

3. **`src/motorcycle.ts`.** `Motorcycle extends Travel`. It needs no
   constructor of its own, because the one in `Travel` already takes exactly
   the distance. Its `description` is the plain word `Motorcycle`, and
   `Bicycle` and `Walk` below follow that pattern with their own names.

4. **`src/bicycle.ts`.** `Bicycle extends Motorcycle`, because above 1 km the
   money is the same. Override `reimbursement()` to return `0` for a distance
   of 1 km or less, and to return `super.reimbursement()` otherwise. Override
   `description` too.

5. **`src/walk.ts`.** `Walk extends Travel` with its own rate of `0.38` and
   the same 1 km limit.

6. **`src/index.ts`.** Same shape as the shapes calculator: stylesheet, the
   nine elements with a null check, `const travels: Travel[] = [];`, a
   `render` helper that rebuilds `#travelList` from `summary()` and writes the
   total into `#totalReimbursement`, and six listeners. Read the distance with
   `distanceInput.valueAsNumber`.

7. **Test with this sequence.** Type the distance, then click the button, in
   this order:

   | Button | Distance | Line shows |
   | --- | ---: | ---: |
   | Car | 10 | 5.00 € |
   | Car, 1 extra passenger | 10 | 5.15 € |
   | Car, 2 extra passengers | 10 | 5.30 € |
   | Bicycle | 10 | 2.50 € |
   | Bicycle | 0.75 | 0.00 € |
   | Walk | 0.75 | 0.00 € |

   The total must end at `17.95`. If it does not, the line that is wrong tells
   you which class to open.

8. **Run `npm run verify`** and fix what it reports.

::: {.callout-tip}
## When you finish early

Empty the distance field and click a button. `valueAsNumber` hands you `NaN`,
and the whole list turns into `NaN €`. Catch it with `Number.isNaN` before you
create the travel, and refuse a negative distance in the same `if`.
:::
